This is the value of the area when `h=3`, not the rate of change of the area.

The definite integral was correctly used to find a net change given a rate of change, but incorrectly uses the `text(3-hour)` period from `t=0` to `t=3` by not adjusting for the variable t representing the time since `text(5:00 A.M.)`
`int_0^3s(t)dt`

This is the average value of the rate at which sand is being added over the interval `2<=t<=5`:

The type of discontinuity was misidentified. Since `lim_(x->10^(-))=lim_(x->10^(+))~~0.5`, there is no jump discontinuity at `x=10`. The function is defined at `x=10` and has a removable discontinuity there.

Content: Let f be a differentiable function such that `f(1)=pi` and `f'(x)=sqrt(x^3+6)`. What is the value of `f(5)`?

Key.Rationale: A misunderstanding of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus resulted in computing `f(1)+int_1^5f''(x)dx`.
Computing `f(1)+f'(5)` shows a misunderstanding of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

A common error is to neglect to use the initial condition and just calculate `f(5)=int_1^5sqrt(x^3+6)dx`. This may arise from a misunderstanding of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus or just forgetting to add the initial condition after computing the definite integral with the calculator.
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, `f(5)-f(1)=int_1^5f'(x)dx`. Therefore `f(5)=f(1)+int_1^5sqrt(x^3+6)dx=pi+24.672~~27.814`.

The expression `R(t)=f(t)-g(t)` indicates the rate of change of the number of people in the building (rate in minus rate out). If the derivative `R'(t)=f'(t)-g'(t)` is positive, then `R(t)` is increasing, i.e. the rate of change of the number of people in the building is increasing.

Since velocity is the derivative of position, a positive value of `v` at `t=1` means that `x` is increasing, i.e. the particle is moving to the right. Since acceleration is the derivative of velocity, a positive value of `v'` at `t=1` means that the particle is moving with positive acceleration.

Content: A tire that is leaking air has an initial air pressure of `30` `text(pounds per square inch)` (`text(psi)`). The function `t=f(p)` models the amount of time `t`, in `text(hours)`, it takes for the air pressure of the tire to reach `p` `text(psi)`. What are the units for `f'(p)`?

Key.Rationale: This is the units of the dependent variable only.
This is the units of the independent variable only.

The dependent and independent variables were inverted. While in many problems time is often the independent variable, in this model time is specified as a function of the air pressure and hence is the dependent variable. That is why it is important to understand the functional notation  `t=f(p)`.

The derivative of the function `t=f(p)` is the limit of the difference quotient `(Deltat)/(Deltap)`. The units on the dependent variable, `t`, in the numerator is `text(hours)` and the units on the independent variable, `p`, in the denominator is `text(psi)`. The rate of change, therefore, has units in `text(hours per psi)`.

Content: The `text(first)` derivative of the function `f` is defined by `f'(x)=(x+2e^-x)/(x^2+0.7)`. On what intervals is `f` increasing?

Key.Rationale: A common error is to answer the question as if the graph drawn on the calculator were the graph of the function `f`, not the graph of the derivative `f'`. The function `f'` is increasing between its local minimum and its local maximum, and this interval appears to match the location of those `text(two)` points. The precise values can be found by solving for where `f''(x)=0`.

There may have been confusion about which property of the derivative provides information about where the function is increasing. If `text(one)` believes that the desired property is where the graph of `f`' is concave up, then these `text(two)` intervals appear to work. The precise values of the endpoints can be found by solving for where `f'''(x)=0`.

The function `f` will be increasing where `f`' is positive. The graph of `f'` is always positive on the interval `-2<=x<=1`. This is therefore the best choice.
[One cannot verify graphically that `f'` is positive for `-oo<x<oo`. The denominator in the formula for `f'` is always positive. The numerator is clearly positive for `x>=0` . For `x<0`, observe that the graph of `2e^(-x)` is concave up and therefore lies above the tangent line at `x=0`. This tangent line is `y=2-2x`. Hence `2e^(-x)>2-2x> -x` since `x<0<2`.]

D.Choice: There are no intervals on which `f` is increasing.

Key.Rationale: There may have been confusion about which sign of the derivative provides information about the increasing behavior of the function. Or the observation that there are no `text(zeros)` of `f'` might incorrectly suggest that there are no intervals to investigate.

Content: problems/AP16CABb/media/90a.jpg

The function `h` is defined on the closed interval `[-1,3]`. The graph of `h` , the derivative of `h`, is shown above. The graph consists of `text(two)` semicircles with a common endpoint at `x=1`. Which of the following statements about `h` must be true?

:ibox:`text(I)`. `h(-1)=h(3)`

`text(II)`. `h` is continuous at `x=1`.

`text(III)`. The graph of `h` has a vertical asymptote at `x=1`.

Key.Rationale: It does not recognize that statement `text(II)` is true.

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, `h(3)=h(-1)+int_-1^3h'(x)dx`. Since the region between the graph of `h'` and the `xtext(-axis)` has more area above the axis than below the axis, the definite integral `int_-1^3h'(x)dx` is positive. Therefore `h(3)>h(-1)` and statement `text(I)` is false. The graph shows that derivative of `h` exists on the interval `(-1,3)`. That means that the function h is differentiable on `(-1,3)`, and is therefore continuous on that interval. In particular, `h` is continuous at `x=1`, so statement `text(II)` must be true. Because `h` is continuous at `x=1` and `h'(1)~~0.5`, the graph of h has a tangent line at `x=1` that is not vertical. Locally near `x=1` the graph of `h` will look like that tangent line and thus there cannot be a vertical asymptote at `x=1`. Therefore statement III is false.

Statement I might be chosen by interpreting the given graph as the graph of `h` rather than its derivative. It might also be chosen by recognizing that `h(3)-h(-1)=int_-1^3h'(x)dx` but believing that the symmetry of the areas within the semicircles results in a net change of `0` for `h` over the interval `-1<=x<=3`.

Statement `text(I)` might be chosen for the same reasons as the correct option. Statement `text(III)` might be chosen by interpreting the given graph as the graph of `h` rather than its derivative and confusing vertical asymptote with vertical tangent, or by thinking that the vertical tangent on `h'` at `x=1` results in a vertical asymptote on `h` at `x=1`.
